section_summary: This section documents U.S. government monitoring of suspected Japanese espionage, intelligence gathering, military photography, and propaganda in the United States and abroad during 1933–1935, with later filing annotations. Reports concern alleged spy rings, surveillance of ports and industrial facilities, approaches to naval personnel, requests for infrastructure maps, and Japanese travelers or officials carrying cameras. A substantial memorandum analyzes the evolution of Japanese propaganda from direct government subsidies to subtler private and quasi-official channels. The final pages focus heavily on the arrest, questioning, and release of Japanese naval inspector Yoshio Matsuda in St. Petersburg, Florida.

subfiles.title: Translation from the Nippu Jiji concerning Major Kobayashi
subfiles.about: Reports Major Masasuke Kobayashi's return to San Francisco with an imperial donation and an educational book for Japanese-American children.
subfiles.summary: Kobayashi had spent about a year in Japan consulting government officials, politicians, and industrialists about Japanese education in the United States. He intended to translate and publish a book affirming the righteousness of the Imperial House for use in Japanese grammar schools.

subfiles.title: FBI file-return notation
subfiles.about: Records the return of a letter and its enclosures to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that the material bearing the file number was returned to the Federal Bureau of Investigation through the Office of Security. It is a later administrative filing record rather than a substantive intelligence report.

subfiles.title: Internal note on the Kearny arrests and Japanese Government Railways
subfiles.about: Highlights conclusions from an agent's report on five Japanese arrested at Kearny and an allegation about Japanese Government Railways.
subfiles.summary: The note says the full special-agent report need not be read because its conclusions appear near the end. It particularly flags the claim that the New York office of the Japanese Government Railways was headquarters for a Japanese espionage system.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of J. L. Dalton's report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of a report on five Japanese arrested at Kearny, New Jersey.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Hoover for forwarding Special Agent J. L. Dalton's February 15 report. The report concerned the January 16 arrest of five Japanese by Kearny police.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to the apprehension of Lieutenant Yoshiro Kanamoto
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a Navy Department letter about the reported apprehension of a Japanese assistant naval attaché for air.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references file 701.9411/801. It identifies the subject as Lieutenant Yoshiro Kanamoto of the Japanese Embassy in Washington.

subfiles.title: Second FBI file-return notation
subfiles.about: Records the return of another letter and its enclosures to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The notation states that the material was returned to the Federal Bureau of Investigation through the Office of Security. It documents later custody of the file.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Justice Department information on Japanese activities
subfiles.about: Thanks Hoover for forwarding excerpts from a New York special agent's memorandum on Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Hoover's March 6 letter quoting a memorandum by a Division of Investigation special agent in New York. He expresses the State Department's appreciation for the information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Finnish information on a Japanese spy ring
subfiles.about: Points to a Finland file concerning claims by Finnish political police about a Japanese spy ring in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers readers to file 861.20260d/24. Its subject is allegedly definite Finnish information about an important Japanese espionage network.

subfiles.title: Finnish police offer information on a Japanese spy ring
subfiles.about: Reports that Finnish political police possess information about an important Japanese spy ring in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Finnish authorities wished either to send an agent to Washington or receive an American agent in Helsinki. They also offered to send written information directly to responsible U.S. counterespionage officials if given a name and address.

subfiles.title: Identification of an alleged spy-ring leader in Connecticut
subfiles.about: Adds that Finnish police claim to know the identity and whereabouts of the alleged Japanese spy-ring leader.
subfiles.summary: Albright confirms that the word “Japanese” in the preceding telegram was correct. The Finnish political-police chief claimed that the leader was then in Connecticut.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference requesting Finnish espionage information
subfiles.about: References a telegram asking Finnish authorities to make their information on the alleged Japanese spy ring available.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies telegram number 8, sent at 2 p.m. on March 21. It connects the request with the confidential Finland file.

subfiles.title: Routing note marking material as of possible interest
subfiles.about: Forwards attached intelligence material as possibly useful.
subfiles.summary: The short internal note characterizes the attached item as being of possible interest. Much of the addressee's name is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Internal comment on William Herbert Greene's story
subfiles.about: Introduces a Naval Attaché report about Greene and discusses whether he might be in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The writer calls Greene's story amazing but notes that the Naval Attaché in London understood the danger of moving too quickly. The memorandum says temporary-admission records were kept at ports of entry rather than centrally by the State or Labor Departments.

subfiles.title: Naval Attaché report on Japanese recruitment of William Herbert Greene
subfiles.about: Reports Greene's claim that the Japanese Naval Attaché sought to employ him as an intelligence agent and his offer to double-cross Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene said he knew Captain Oka and had discussed being placed abroad in a business position while serving Japanese intelligence. The U.S. Naval Attaché found Greene's offer extraordinary and could not determine whether he was unstable or sincere, although Greene plainly knew Oka and the Japanese Club. British consulates were asked to watch for his visa application, while the report distinguished him from a different W. H. Green already holding a U.S. visa.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.about: Provides an internal distribution and routing list for intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists War Department, Navy, State, and Commerce offices that might receive the accompanying information. It contains options for filing, noting, returning, or forwarding the material.

subfiles.title: War Department extract on Japanese activity in Arizona and Sonora
subfiles.from: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards claims about Japanese mining specialists in Arizona and unusual Japanese activity in Sonora.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that Kiyoshi Oda and S. Suiy toured Arizona mining installations and methods. It also relays observations of increasing Japanese presence in Sonora and a claim that two Japanese marched from Caborca to San Luis to test the effects of such a journey.

subfiles.title: Report on Captain Hironishi Yohara's photography in Delaware
subfiles.about: Reports Yohara's arrest and allegations that he photographed industrial plants around Newark, Delaware.
subfiles.summary: Delaware police arrested Captain Yohara for driving without a permit. Local authorities further alleged that he photographed industrial sites and mailed thirty-five to fifty photographic postcards to Japan each month.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment concerning Captain Yohara
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report about Yohara's arrest and alleged industrial photography.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck notes that the same information was being supplied to the Office of Naval Intelligence. He thanks Hoover for bringing the matter to the State Department's attention.

subfiles.title: Anonymous warning about sabotage and Japanese spies
subfiles.about: Claims Japanese spies were gathering shipbuilding information and planning sabotage in New York and at the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: The anonymous writer alleged that four spies were operating around Kearny and Camden and that mines had been stored beneath a Japanese steamship dock on the East River. The letter also described a supposed plan to bomb the Holland Tunnel with explosives hidden in cabbages and asserted that the Panama Canal would be Japan's first objective.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to the Greene espionage report
subfiles.about: Points to a report concerning British subject William Herbert Greene's alleged Japanese espionage activity.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references another file containing a copy of the Naval Attaché's report from London. It characterizes Greene as apparently engaged in espionage on behalf of Japan.

subfiles.title: Handwritten departmental routing notation
subfiles.about: Records internal handling of intelligence correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR is largely illegible but includes an April 23 notation and routing initials. It appears to be an administrative slip rather than a substantive report.

subfiles.title: Hoover transmittal concerning Ryo Ohara
subfiles.about: Transmits Shelby Wishart's letter about Japanese artist Ryo Ohara of Evansville.
subfiles.summary: Hoover identifies Ohara as a longtime Karges Furniture Company employee who had recently disappeared from Evansville. He forwards Wishart's April 9 account as potentially interesting to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Shelby Wishart's report on Ryo Ohara
subfiles.to: Department of Investigation, Department of Justice
subfiles.about: Describes conversations and circumstances that led Wishart to suspect furniture artist Ryo Ohara of intelligence work.
subfiles.summary: Wishart portrays Ohara as exceptionally informed about international affairs, fortifications, Japanese policy, and the locations of Japanese students. He recounts a telegram from the South Manchurian Railway Company that sent Ohara urgently to Chicago to see Mr. Wu before his departure for New York. Ohara's unexplained disappearance after years in Evansville strengthened Wishart's belief that he was not merely a furniture decorator.

subfiles.title: McGrath letter forwarding Lands End observations
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of two observation reports that McGrath believed had not reached government officials.
subfiles.summary: McGrath tells President Roosevelt that the enclosed letters might be of interest. The file notes that copies also went to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Observation of a Japanese man surveying the Golden Gate
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese man making an optical survey of coastal lands and forts at the Golden Gate.
subfiles.summary: McGrath observed the man for about thirty minutes as he studied the coastline, fortifications, and papers in a portfolio. The man carried an officer-style cap and returned to his observation point as though checking his conclusions.

subfiles.title: Observation of three men surveying the Sutro property
subfiles.about: Reports three apparent foreigners examining and measuring property adjoining Lands End.
subfiles.summary: The men arrived by automobile with a map of the Sutro property and surveyed both the exterior and interior while citing dimensions. McGrath remembered seeing two of them inspect the property about two weeks earlier.

subfiles.title: Hoover transmittal of the Gritzner report
subfiles.about: Forwards Charles Fred Gritzner's report of an unnamed Japanese traveler whom he suspected of espionage.
subfiles.summary: Gritzner encountered the man on an April 28 train from Key West to Miami. Hoover transmits the April 30 letter as being of possible interest to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Gritzner's account of an unnamed Japanese traveler
subfiles.about: Describes a drunken Japanese traveler whose remarks led fellow passengers to suspect that he was a spy.
subfiles.summary: The traveler said he had a pass valid in any country, was paid despite having no apparent business, and was heading to Washington before touring the United States. He criticized American social cohesion, predicted regret over recognition of Russia, and spoke English, Spanish, and Japanese.

subfiles.title: Internal note on obtaining further information
subfiles.about: Suggests asking the Department of Justice for further information about the unidentified traveler.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten note is poorly preserved in OCR. Its discernible portion proposes an inquiry to the Department of Justice similar to an earlier request.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence request to identify the Key West traveler
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department can identify the unnamed Japanese traveler reported at Key West.
subfiles.summary: Logan refers to the Justice Department's May 22 letter about the alleged spy. The Office of Naval Intelligence wanted the individual's name if it could be determined.

subfiles.title: 1937 note forwarding an older propaganda memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards an approximately three-year-old memorandum on Japanese propaganda for review.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten note introduces the attached study of Japanese propaganda. It appears to ask whether the recipient has seen it and to comment on its continued relevance.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the evolution of Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Analyzes changes in Japanese government and private propaganda methods since 1921.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum credits Frederick Moore and Dallas McGrew with modernizing Japanese Foreign Office press work and describes the Bureau of Intelligence's relations with journalists. It compares Kokusai with the more discreetly organized Rengo News Agency and discusses War and Navy press offices, subsidized newspapers, advertising, and privately financed publicists. It concludes that private individuals and quasi-official bodies increasingly carried the costs and execution of propaganda while the Japanese Government continued to shape its content.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary letter and attached list concerning Japanese visitors
subfiles.about: A fragmentary communication appears to report Japanese visitors taking photographs and supplies a list of names or contacts.
subfiles.summary: The OCR mentions a conference, photographs, and a large hotel or site that could be watched by air, but much of the wording is unreadable. The following page lists several names and abbreviated locations, including J. Sakurai and New York references.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to D. F. Giera's alleged secret-agent claim
subfiles.about: References a memorandum reporting Giera's statement that he was a secret agent of the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to file 811.113/381 3/7. It identifies the source as the Division of Western European Affairs.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to alleged solicitation of U.S. naval personnel
subfiles.about: References a Tsingtao despatch about a Japanese cabaret girl's alleged effort to obtain information from U.S. sailors.
subfiles.summary: The referenced material includes a statement by Machinist's Mate Stuart Johnson to Vice Consul Hawthorne. It concerns intelligence approaches to American naval personnel in China.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch forwarding Stuart Johnson's statement
subfiles.from: David C. Berger, American Consul, Tsingtao
subfiles.about: Transmits Vice Consul Hawthorne's memorandum of a statement by U.S. sailor Stuart Johnson.
subfiles.summary: Berger forwards the memorandum as potentially interesting to the Department. Johnson was a Machinist's Mate Second Class in the U.S. Navy.

subfiles.title: Hawthorne memorandum on intelligence approaches to U.S. sailors
subfiles.about: Records Johnson's warning that sailors treated as foreign or alien were especially vulnerable to foreign intelligence approaches.
subfiles.summary: Johnson described resentment among sailors of immigrant background and said a woman in a Shanghai cabaret tried to elicit submarine information from him. He also reported finding three intoxicated sailors in a Japanese cabaret with the mistress of the resident Japanese naval intelligence officer. He recommended conclusively establishing the citizenship of naval personnel, especially before service abroad.

subfiles.title: Justice Department transmittal of Phelan's suspicions
subfiles.about: Forwards William D. Phelan's suggestion that Japanese shops in New York might conceal improper activity.
subfiles.summary: Keenan offers to arrange an investigation if the State Department considers the matter important. The enclosure consists of Phelan's letter and newspaper clipping.

subfiles.title: Phelan letter alleging Japanese commercial fronts
subfiles.about: Suggests that fashionable Japanese shops in New York may be fronts for espionage.
subfiles.summary: Phelan cites a newspaper column and recalls claims that Japanese barbers in the Panama Canal Zone were engaged in espionage. On that basis, he urges investigation of Japanese shops in New York.

subfiles.title: Assessment of Japanese shops on Fifth Avenue
subfiles.about: Identifies the established Japanese shops likely referenced in Phelan's complaint and finds them reputable.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum distinguishes numerous wholesale importers from the fashionable retailers Yamanaka and Yamatoya. It describes Yamanaka as a renowned international antique dealer and notes that Yamatoya had once been patronized by Mr. Stimson.

subfiles.title: State Department reply declining a broad investigation of Japanese shops
subfiles.from: William Phillips for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Declines to recommend a concerted investigation without substantial prima facie evidence of improper activity.
subfiles.summary: The Department warns that a sweeping inquiry into foreign-owned commercial enterprises could harm relations with the country concerned. It offers to reconsider if specific evidence implicating Japanese stores in New York becomes available.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum of S-43's sabotage warning
subfiles.from: S-43 via Mr. Jacobs and Miss Laser
subfiles.about: Records an anonymous caller's sweeping allegations of Japanese military organization, sabotage plans, and illegal fortification.
subfiles.summary: S-43 claimed Japanese agents and disguised laborers were being organized and drilled throughout major cities and along the West Coast. He predicted attacks on ammunition dumps, coast artillery, antiaircraft defenses, and air squadrons, and alleged that the Bonin Islands were eighty percent fortified. He urged strict exclusion of Japanese people from ports, military sites, carriers, and airfields and tighter controls on aircraft sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to a proposed Japanese information library
subfiles.about: References Herbert S. Houston's proposal that Japan establish an information library in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Houston suggested such a library to acquaint Americans with Japanese affairs. The sheet directs readers to file 894.428/7.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary Los Angeles letter to the President
subfiles.about: A poorly legible letter appears to raise concerns about allowing Japanese access to American inventions or processes.
subfiles.summary: The letter was acknowledged by form and filed in October 1934. Its surviving text suggests concern over technical information reaching Japan, apparently in connection with the accompanying clipping.

subfiles.title: Clipping on sales and technical information supplied to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Senate testimony about American arms sales, patent information, and Japanese efforts to obtain manufacturing data.
subfiles.summary: Federal Laboratories president John W. Young testified about proposed sales to Japan and said Japanese commercial services systematically sought American patent numbers. The article also discusses Colonel M. P. Smoot, Patricia Kendall, tear-gas sales, and offers by American firms to train foreign forces in chemical warfare. Senator Gerald P. Nye questioned whether such commerce conflicted with U.S. defense planning against a possible war with Japan.

subfiles.title: Navy transmittal of a message about oil-company maps
subfiles.about: Forwards a naval-district message about a Japanese request for California oil-infrastructure maps.
subfiles.summary: Canaga says the information will interest Hornbeck. He indicates that the oil companies' request will be denied.

subfiles.title: Naval message concerning Nissho Company's map request
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: Reports that Nissho Company sought maps of California pipelines and oil facilities on behalf of the Japanese Navy.
subfiles.summary: Union Oil informed the naval district that Nissho had approached Union, Richfield, and Standard Oil. The message recommends informing the companies of the Navy Department's wishes while protecting the source's confidentiality.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the California pipeline-map report
subfiles.about: Thanks Canaga for the message concerning Japanese efforts to obtain oil-infrastructure maps.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck confirms that the State Department read the Eleventh Naval District report with interest. He expresses appreciation for the Navy's courtesy in sharing it.

subfiles.title: Immigration Service account of Murakami and Higashi's detention
subfiles.from: W. W. Brown, Immigration and Naturalization Service
subfiles.about: Explains the brief Miami police detention of two Japanese nationals suspected because they photographed the waterfront.
subfiles.summary: Immigration Inspector Gray found Yasunori Murakami and Yoshitane Higashi lawfully present and advised that the Immigration Service had no jurisdictional interest. Miami police released them after about an hour, and no formal immigration report was initially considered necessary.

subfiles.title: Miami police report on Murakami and Higashi
subfiles.from: L. O. Scarboro, by Detective Sergeant E. Melchen
subfiles.about: Reports the questioning and itinerary of two Japanese railway engineers accused of photographing transportation facilities.
subfiles.summary: Complaints alleged that the men photographed Miami's harbor, docks, railroad station, and airports. Police verified their passports, identified them as civil engineers for the Imperial Railways of Japan, and allowed them to continue to Key West and then New York.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese Naval Attaché press activity
subfiles.about: References a Navy Department letter about statements to the American press by the Japanese Naval Attaché.
subfiles.summary: The statements concerned Japan's position on abrogation of the Naval Limitations Treaty. The referenced file included a pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese espionage reports in the Aleutians
subfiles.from: Far Eastern Division, Department of State
subfiles.about: References a memorandum assessing alleged Japanese espionage in the Aleutian Islands.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reportedly concluded that available State Department information did not show activities of a serious nature. The sheet directs readers to file 894.628/117.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese fishing vessels and naval exercises
subfiles.about: References concerns that Japanese fishing vessels observed U.S. fleet exercises and communicated with Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: The referenced Navy letter noted long-range radios and crew members who did not appear to be fishermen. It advised against using Japanese vessels to transship lobster catches from Los Angeles to Japan.

subfiles.title: Initial memorandum on Yoshio Matsuda's arrest
subfiles.about: Summarizes Labor Department information on Matsuda's arrest and release in St. Petersburg.
subfiles.summary: Matsuda was arrested by local police as a suspicious person and questioned by immigration officials for roughly two hours. Labor officials said he was no longer in custody and were checking his Seattle entry record, while noting a Tokyo visa report identifying him as a naval inspector and lieutenant commander.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on interdepartmental handling of the Matsuda incident
subfiles.about: Reports conversations with Labor and Naval Intelligence officials about Matsuda's arrest and official status.
subfiles.summary: Colonel MacCormack said a Justice Department agent apparently prompted the arrest but praised the immigration officer who arranged Matsuda's release. The writer supplied MacCormack and Captain Puleston with State Department records showing that Matsuda had received an official visa in Tokyo in October 1933. Labor did not anticipate further action.

subfiles.title: Press statement on Yoshio Matsuda
subfiles.about: Explains Matsuda's naval status, lawful entry claim, and release from local custody.
subfiles.summary: The statement identifies Matsuda as a Japanese naval constructor and lieutenant commander assigned as a naval inspector in New York. It says the immigration examination was routine and that he was released after his legal status was established, pending confirmation from Seattle.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Matsuda's immigration status
subfiles.about: Sets out Matsuda's arrival, visa class, occupation, destination, and intended stay.
subfiles.summary: Matsuda arrived at Seattle aboard the Hikawa Maru on November 6, 1933. He held a government-official visa issued in Tokyo, described himself as a chief naval constructor, and gave the Japanese Naval Inspector's Office in New York as his destination.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping on Matsuda's arrest
subfiles.from: New York Times and Associated Press
subfiles.about: Reports Matsuda's arrest while photographing the St. Petersburg waterfront and the USS Trenton.
subfiles.summary: Police portrayed Matsuda as a possible spy equipped with long-range still and motion-picture cameras and quoted him as saying the Japanese Navy financed him. The article traces an alleged photographic itinerary through several Atlantic cities, while his New York landlady described him as a gentleman. Japanese Consul General Renzo Sawada said he did not recognize the name.

subfiles.title: New York Herald Tribune clipping on Matsuda's photography
subfiles.from: New York Herald Tribune and Associated Press
subfiles.about: Gives another press account of Matsuda's alleged photography of Eastern ports.
subfiles.summary: The article repeats police claims that Matsuda photographed principal seaports and sent developed film from New York to Japan. It records contradictory statements about his naval rank, identity papers, Columbia University association, and recommendation by the Japanese Embassy.

subfiles.title: Routing note on the Labor Department's Matsuda memorandum
subfiles.about: Identifies the attached Labor Department memorandum as an account of the Matsuda incident.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten notation says the memorandum detailing the incident involving a Japanese naval officer at St. Petersburg came from the Labor Department that morning. It serves as a cover note for the following report.

subfiles.title: Immigration memorandum detailing Matsuda's arrest and release
subfiles.about: Reconstructs the actions of police and immigration officers during Matsuda's detention and release.
subfiles.summary: A Justice Department agent prompted Jacksonville immigration officials to investigate Matsuda after St. Petersburg police arrested him. Tampa officers examined him, recognized the diplomatic sensitivity of detaining a claimed Japanese naval purchasing officer, and arranged his release into Patrol Inspector Roux's care. Seattle records then confirmed his November 1933 admission with a government-official visa and assignment to the Japanese Naval Inspector's Office in New York.

subfiles.title: Photographic clipping: Cameraman Non Grata
subfiles.about: Captions a photograph of Matsuda and summarizes his detention for photographing southern harbors and a U.S. cruiser.
subfiles.summary: The caption identifies Matsuda as a lieutenant commander in the Japanese Navy. It notes that he was released without prosecution but was expected to explain himself to the Japanese Embassy.

subfiles.title: State Department note on preparing a reply concerning Matsuda
subfiles.about: Reviews the need for a fuller factual record before replying to Japanese representations about Matsuda's treatment.
subfiles.summary: The writer requested a comprehensive statement from Deputy Commissioner Wixon after reviewing memoranda and a conversation between the Japanese Counselor and Mr. Turner. Mr. Ward believed Matsuda's conduct reasonably aroused suspicion and that the brief detention was defensible until his official status was confirmed. The memorandum continues beyond page 160.
